title: Sell Mineral Rights in Michigan
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Michigan | Antrim Legacy
metaDescription: Antrim shale gas check from the 1990s boom, or Niagaran reef legacy oil? Michigan interests are mostly mature. We buy them and explain the offer clearly.
heroLead: If you've been holding a Michigan royalty interest since the 1990s, there is a decent chance you signed that lease during the original Antrim shale gas rush, long before shale drilling was a household term anywhere else.
intro: Michigan's Antrim shale, concentrated in the northern lower peninsula around Otsego and Grand Traverse counties, was one of the earliest large-scale shale gas developments in the country, drilled hard through the 1990s using vertical wells and coalbed-style dewatering, well before horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing became the industry standard elsewhere. That makes Michigan's shale history genuinely older than most owners realize.

There is also a separate, even older legacy in the Michigan basin's Niagaran reef trend, small isolated oil and gas reservoirs scattered across the northern lower peninsula that have been quietly producing since the 1970s and 80s. Between the two, most Michigan mineral owners are sitting on production that peaked decades ago and has been sliding gradually ever since.

sections.heading: The Antrim Boom Is Thirty Years in the Rearview
paragraphs: Antrim wells were drilled in a concentrated wave and, like most dewatering plays, took a few years to ramp to peak gas production before beginning a long decline. Most of those wells are now decades past their peak, producing a fraction of their original rate on a well-worn, predictable curve.

New Antrim drilling essentially stopped years ago as the play matured and operators moved on. If your check has been shrinking slowly for a long time without any sudden change, that tracks with exactly what this field has been doing for a generation.

sections.heading: Reading an Antrim Statement
paragraphs: Antrim wells produce both gas and, notably, a fair amount of water, since dewatering the shale is what releases the gas in the first place. Water handling costs are a normal, recurring line item here, and they do not indicate a well is failing, just that it is doing what Antrim wells have always done.

Because these are older wells on older leases, it is also worth checking whether your specific lease predates common modern post-production cost language, since that can meaningfully change how deductions are calculated relative to a lease signed today.

sections.heading: Niagaran Reef Interests Are a Quieter Story
paragraphs: Niagaran reef fields are smaller and more isolated than Antrim, individual reservoirs rather than one continuous formation, so production and decline can vary quite a bit from field to field even within the same county. Some of these fields have been producing steadily since the 1970s and 80s with very little fanfare.

If your interest is tied to one of these older reef fields, we look at the specific well's history rather than treating it like a typical Antrim interest, since the two production profiles do not necessarily move together.

sections.heading: Selling a Legacy Michigan Interest
paragraphs: For most Michigan owners, the question is straightforward: the well is well past its peak, new drilling is not a realistic factor, and the choice comes down to a small but stable check continuing on the same gradual decline versus a lump sum today.

We build the offer from your actual recent statements, confirm ownership against the county register of deeds, most commonly in the northern lower peninsula counties where these fields sit, and typically close within a few weeks.

faqs.question: Why does your Antrim shale statement show a water disposal charge?
faqs.answer: Antrim wells produce alongside significant water volumes because dewatering the shale is what releases the trapped gas. That cost is a standard, ongoing part of how these wells operate, not a sign of a problem.

faqs.question: Is anyone still drilling new Antrim wells in Michigan?
faqs.answer: New drilling in the Antrim slowed to essentially nothing years ago as the play matured. Current production comes almost entirely from wells drilled during the original 1990s development wave.

faqs.question: What is a Niagaran reef and how is it different from Antrim?
faqs.answer: Niagaran reef fields are isolated, individual oil and gas reservoirs scattered across Michigan's northern lower peninsula, distinct from the continuous Antrim shale formation. Production history can vary significantly from one reef field to the next.

faqs.question: Your check has been the same small amount for years. Is that normal?
faqs.answer: For a mature Antrim or Niagaran interest, yes. These are old, slow-decline fields, and a small, fairly stable check is consistent with a well many years past its original peak.

faqs.question: What should an owner do after inheriting a Michigan interest without receiving statements?
faqs.answer: Reach out to the operator listed on any old paperwork you have to confirm whether the well is still producing and whether your ownership was ever updated after the interest passed to you. We can help identify the operator from an old lease or division order if you are not sure.

faqs.question: Are Antrim leases from the 1990s different from modern leases?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Many Antrim-era leases predate the standardized post-production cost and deduction language common in leases written today, so it is worth confirming what your specific lease actually says before assuming how deductions should be calculated.
